abstract: the models of modified gravity that can explain the late-time accelerated expansion of the universe must pass the local tests of gravity, introducing a screening mechanism so that any additional fifth force in gravity is suppressed at stellar scales. dark matter halos, in contrast, by their extendedness in scale, may exhibit a transition of screening to small scales, providing a probe of modified gravity and the origin of the late-time acceleration. we perform comprehensive studies of dark matter halos with vainshtein screening in the horndeski theory. given that dark matter is cold and a dark matter halo is spherically symmetric, we analytically clarify the conditions for the halo profile under which the vainshtein screening works effectively. we find that the vainshtein screening is less effective even within the vainshtein radius as the profile approaches a core-like structure around the center of a halo, which motivates us to postulate that some features owing to the fifth force can survive during the dynamical evolution of a halo. we numerically examine our postulate by a $n$-body simulation for an isolated halo with the assumption of newtonian two-body interactions with the spherical external fifth force. we make use of three proxies of the mass through hydrostatic dynamics, the jeans equation, and gravitational lensing, all of which must be identical in the case of newtonian gravity as a weak-field approximation to general relativity. we find that these proxies can be biased relative to each other at a (quasi) equilibrium, quantitatively indicating that the fiducial model of gravity is not newtonian. our result affirmatively suggests that multiple mass proxies from observations are capable of testing gravity on halo scales.

title: environment-induced topological reconstruction of black-hole thermodynamics
abstract: thermodynamic topology describes black-hole (bh) equilibria as zeros, or defects, of a vector field built from the off-shell free energy. studies with surrounding matter find that the topological class is unchanged, but not how the matter's spatial distribution affects individual equilibria. we ask whether the position of a localized environment can reorganize these equilibria at fixed total topological number. we model the environment as a radially localized energy bump peaked at $a_m$ and add its exterior energy to the generalized off-shell free energy. as $a_m$ varies, defects migrate and are created or annihilated in opposite-charge pairs, a process we call topological reconstruction. it changes the number and stability of equilibrium branches but preserves the total topological number, provided no zero crosses the boundary of the physical domain. we find this in schwarzschild, schwarzschild-ads, reissner-nordström, and reissner-nordström-ads bhs, with critical positions and required strength that depend on the background. in our examples, the required environmental energy ranges from below $1\%$ of the bh mass to a value comparable to it. the model is an effective fixed-background description without backreaction. within it, the total topological number cannot capture the environmental response; local defects must be tracked.

title: uniqueness of static black holes in lovelock gravity
abstract: black hole uniqueness is one of the fundamental predictions of general relativity: the spherically symmetric schwarzschild--tangherlini spacetime is the unique regular, asymptotically flat, static vacuum black hole solution of einstein's equations. we show that an analogous result holds perturbatively in lovelock gravity. assuming the appropriate positive-mass rigidity statement, any regular, asymptotically flat, static vacuum black hole solution of lovelock gravity on a generic branch admitting a regular taylor expansion about general relativity is uniquely determined, at fixed adm mass, by the corresponding spherically symmetric lovelock black hole solution. in particular, einstein--gauss--bonnet gravity admits no distinct nonspherical static branch perturbatively connected to schwarzschild--tangherlini, and the unique solution is boulware--deser. the same recursive mechanism extends to the full lovelock class. our result shows that static black hole uniqueness can extend beyond general relativity and is not a property peculiar to the einstein equations.

title: conservative orbital resonance networks as local environmental diagnostics for extreme mass ratio inspirals
abstract: llow order orbital resonances provide localized probes of the conservative geometry sampled by extreme mass ratio inspirals. we study fixed eccentricity and inclination slices of the ordered $3{:}2$, $5{:}3$, and $2{:}1$ polar to radial resonance surfaces in source consistent anisotropic black hole environments, treating rotation strictly to first order. a horizon regularized dehnen sequence produces unequal resonance displacements, reaching $-7.17\%$, $-5.45\%$, and $-3.94\%$ in a fixed global benchmark. after matching both the total environmental mass and the enclosed mass at $10m_\bullet$, we compare dehnen and einasto inspired families. two dimensionless network spacing ratios are organized primarily by the local logarithmic enclosed mass slope: for the common $β=2$ regularization their maximum cross family departure from a shared linear relation is $4.1\times10^{-4}$, while varying the horizon taper through $β=2$--$4$ increases the departure to at most $2.1\times10^{-3}$. the unequal ordering of the three resonance displacements holds at every point of a directly evaluated finite eccentricity and inclination grid. a six observable conservative response analysis is numerically full rank but strongly ill conditioned and nearly aligned with orbital nuisance directions. the result therefore establishes local conservative profile sensitivity, not unique tomography or a detector level parameter recovery forecast.

title: simulating dust collapse: the impact of gauge choices on primordial black hole formation
abstract: we investigate why numerical relativity simulations of dust collapse in a matter-dominated era frequently fail before primordial black hole formation due to numerical limitations and inappropriate gauge choices. using 3-dimensional fully non-linear simulations of a dust fluid, we detail the advantages of advanced numerical methods and the impact of the lapse and shift evolution equations. the challenge is twofold: 1) conventional lapse slicing evolution equations, highly effective in typical black hole simulations, must be adapted in a cosmological context. we demonstrate how different proposed lapse evolution equations perform, enabling fair comparison, and propose our own. 2) the shift evolution equation's role is to spread out the numerical grid observers for a stable simulation. however, the gamma-driver evolution fails when confronted with shell-focussing of the dust fluid. we show how the shift damping choice depends on the resolution of the shell-focusing region, suggesting that future work should have spatially varying damping. our improved gauge choices allow simulations to evolve significantly further and potentially reach black hole formation. the best-performing simulations reach close proximity to a black hole; however, further work on the gauge choice is required for this to be stable.

title: near-extremal black-hole formation observed from null infinity
abstract: we identify near-extremal black-hole formation directly from observables at future null infinity. fully nonlinear evolutions of the spherically symmetric einstein--maxwell--charged scalar system in 3+1 dimensions form black holes with charge-to-mass ratios up to 0.993 from regular, horizon-free, superextremal initial data. quasinormal frequencies and redshift decay independently recover the near-extremal charge-to-mass ratio. critical mass scaling is recovered at null infinity and charge scaling at the apparent horizon. the charged scalar newman--penrose quantity obeys an asymptotic balance law that replaces the conservation law of the neutral theory.
